This will be updated at MTR and TER.Additional details on Gender, Stakeholder Engagement, and safeguards presented below:The Project seeks gender equality and adopts a gender transformative approach. The project conducted a gender assessment and prepared a Gender Action Plan (GAP) to encourage equitable gender participation in all activities. The GAP has been prepared considering gender gaps that can be addressed by the Project and defining monitoring indicators and goals. This assessment reveals significant gender gaps in decision-making instances and in access to financing for collective actions on conservation, sustainable use, or restoration of biodiversity. Hence, the GAP gives emphasis to strengthening the role of women in project activities and the goal is that 50 percent of its beneficiaries are women. The Project aims to enhance participation of women in the community-based governance and sustainable production activities by incorporating actions to (a) strengthen women’s participation and leadership within community decision-making processes, and (b) ensure women get an equitable share of the economic benefits resulting from the sustainable use of the natural resources. Gender-focused activities will include gender assessments, the facilitation of women’s participation in formal and informal decision-making structures and governance processes, and training for capacity strengthening to ensure effective nature-based economic development. Project outcomes will be measured based on three indicators of women’s agency: (a) the number of women participating in decision-making processes regarding Project-supported activities; (b) the number of women who participated in decision-making processes regarding Project-supported activities and who consider that they embody their visions and meet their needs; and (c) the number of women-led organizations and organizations in which at least half of the members are women among the organizations beneficiaries of the Project. The Project’s GAP includes the following pillars: (a) enhance women’s participation in local conservation, community forest management and sustainable production activities; (b) boost the participation of women in decision-making processes related to the management of protected areas supported by the Project; (c) boost the participation of women in decision-making processes at the municipal level; and (d) tackle sexual harassment, abuse, and exploitation and gender-based violence. The Monitoring and Evaluation process of gender actions and indicators will be based on the record of the activities conducted and on primary and secondary data collected during their implementation. There will be three rounds of data collection and analysis throughout the life of the project: (i) in the first year of implementation; (ii) at the midpoint of the implementation period; and (iii) upon conclusion of the Project. The following indicators will be monitored during project implementation, as defined in the GAP: Intermediate indicators monitored in the Brazil ASL Xingu project. Communities and general public engagement in public policy decision-making, planning and implementation will be explicitly supported under the project.The Project Stakeholder Engagement Plan (SEP) comprises the following four fundamental pillars, each aimed at ensuring effective and inclusive stakeholder engagement:Pillar 1 – Identification of stakeholders: Ongoing and evolving stakeholder mapping to ensure all relevant voices are considered.Pillar 2 – Transparency and information disclosure: Sharing relevant information in a clear and accessible manner in order to keep all stakeholders well-informed about project progress and activities.Pillar 3 – Engagement with Stakeholders: Establishment of accessible channels to support dialogue with stakeholders and the public in general while ensuring active and collaborative participation. This pillar includes aspects related to:Critical integration of feedback: Consideration and integration of feedback from stakeholders in the implementation of project activities, in an ongoing adjustment and improvement process.Attention to vulnerable individuals and groups: A special focus on ensuring that the needs and concerns of vulnerable individuals and groups are addressed.Gender issues: Consideration of a gender perspective in all project activities and decisions by promoting equity between men and women. Pillar 4 – Grievance Redress Mechanism (GRM): Implementation of effective mechanisms to respond to and redress grievances in a timely manner in order to ensure satisfaction and trust among stakeholders.These enabling pillars ensure that the SEP is an effective tool for the engagement and participation of all stakeholders by promoting a collaborative and transparent environment throughout the project life cycle. Each of these pillars is further detailed in subsequent chapters.In addition, citizen engagement and participation (through civil society and CBOs) are at the core of the project’s design. Consultations have been held with organizations representing the potential beneficiaries of the Project to define the scope of activities, areas of intervention, and targets of the Project. Furthermore, the SEP sets a robust strategy for continuous and meaningful consultation with Project beneficiaries (and particularly those who belong to disadvantaged and vulnerable social groups), including the creation of spaces for dialogue where members of local communities can express their opinions. Citizen engagement will be monitored and evaluated through two intermediary indicators: (a) number of beneficiaries from local communities who participate in decision-making processes regarding Project-supported activities and consider that they embody their visions and needs, and (b) grievances raised regarding the Project whose resolution was facilitated in an effective and prompt manner. Indicators Targets Number of women who benefit from conservation, sustainable use or biodiversity restoration activities supported by the Project 1500 Proportion of women among participants in decision-making processes regarding activities supported by the Project 40% Proportion of women among female participants in decision-making processes regarding activities supported by the Project who believe that these activities take into consideration their views and meet their needs. 80% Proportion of women-led organizations and organizations where at least half of the members are women among the beneficiary organizations of the Project 40% Proportion of local content on conservation and sustainable production prepared for various media that incorporate gender aspects and women’s perspectives. 80% Proportion of women among the members of the Management Councils of the Conservation Units supported by the Project. 30% The overall Risk Classification for the project is Moderate The Project environmental and social risk is rated as Moderate. The project will generate considerable environmental and social (E&S) benefits through due diligence for strengthening PA management, coordination and implementation of environmental protection policies, and strengthening sustainable natural resource-based production. Key E&S direct/indirect risks/impacts are expected to be moderate, predictable and reversible. They may include: increased natural resource use or risks to forest integrity due to inadequate implementation and/or monitoring of sustainable community forestry or natural resource management plans; temporary site-specific impacts of residue, pollution or resource use from small construction or remodelling works for Protected Areas management and vigilance infrastructure, or natural resource processing units; the minor generation of residues/leftovers by raw materials’ small processing units; water and natural resource use; contamination or erosion from inadequate pest and soil management; restrictions on land/natural resource use; inequitable access to project information/benefits; exposure of highly sensitive vulnerable communities and workers to communicable diseases and SEA/SH incidents. These risks can be prevented or mitigated with the adoption of best practices and adequate measures to be defined in the environmental and social risk management instruments. The Project design already incorporates some measures to prevent and mitigate impacts from timber and non-timber management, such as the provision of technical assistance and support to reviewing and updating Community-based Forest Management Plans, and to meet Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) standards that are environmentally appropriate, socially beneficial, and economically viable. Such measures will be complemented in the environmental and social risk management instruments for the Project, which will be prepared based on the existing ESMF, IPPF and PF of the previous Brazil ASL project (phases 1 and 2), which will be reviewed and updated to assess risks/impacts consistent with the ESSs, define mitigation measures, and screen out activities leading to significant negative impacts on natural/critical habitats, biodiversity, and remote communities no later than 30 days after Effectiveness. The FGV, MMA, ICMBio, SFB, SEMAS and IDEFLOR-Bio have been demonstrating moderately satisfactory or better performance with the Bank’s safeguards through the implementation of the previous operation P158000 Brazil ASL project (phases 1 and 2), which triggered OP 4.01, OP 4.04, OP 4.36, OP 4.09, OP 4.11, OP 4.10 and OP 4.12. Although the Additional Financing (ASL Phase 2) was prepared after 2018, this is the first time the project will be fully implemented under the ESF. Capacity building needs of the executing agency will be addressed in the ESCP, which will also define the number and qualification of Environmental and Social specialists to be assigned to PEU-FGV.
